options: The given value for every row where condition is true — it's the "if" part of the expression
A boolean True or False only, never the actual value
An error if condition is ever false for any row
The average of value across all matching rows
questions.explain: .otherwise(value) is the matching "else" — together they build one column expression.

questions.q: When chaining multiple .when() calls, how are they evaluated?
options: Top to bottom, in order — the first one that matches wins, exactly like an if/elif/else chain
All at once, with the last matching condition winning instead
In a random order each time the DataFrame is read
Only the very first .when() is ever checked, the rest are ignored
questions.explain: This is why order matters — a broader condition checked too early can mislabel rows that a later, narrower condition was meant to catch.

questions.q: What happens to a row that matches no when() condition when there's no .otherwise()?
options: The result is null for that row — not an error, not a default guess
PySpark throws an immediate error and the read fails
The row is silently dropped from the DataFrame entirely
It defaults to the value from the very first when() clause
questions.explain: This is a genuine, easy-to-miss source of unexpected nulls in real pipelines — Lesson 51 covers null handling directly.

questions.q: Why does the order of chained .when() calls matter?
options: Because the first matching condition wins — checking a broader condition too early can incorrectly catch rows meant for a later, narrower one
Order never matters; PySpark evaluates every condition and picks the most specific automatically
Because Python requires when() calls to be alphabetically ordered
It only matters when using numeric conditions, not string comparisons
questions.explain: For example, checking trip_distance > 3 before trip_distance > 10 would mislabel every long trip as merely 'medium'.

questions.q: How does when()/.otherwise() typically get used together with withColumn()?
options: The when()/.otherwise() chain builds a single expression that becomes withColumn()'s second argument
They can never be used together in the same statement
withColumn() must be called twice, once for when() and once for otherwise()
when() replaces withColumn() entirely and is called on its own
questions.explain: This directly reuses the withColumn() pattern from Lesson 46: name, plus an expression describing what goes in it.
